prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how trade and technological change reshape local labour markets, labour demand and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I keep B019 first, with a narrower and more defensible scope than my opening. The contribution answers a first-order question: why adjustment to trade and technology shocks was slower and more geographically concentrated than the standard model implied. It did so with explicit, quasi-experimental designs that independent researchers have re-examined at length. The qualitative result, persistent local adjustment costs, has survived the main critiques as far as I understand them. I have not verified this independently. The China-shock papers are a jointly authored Autor-Dorn-Hanson body of work, so the credit is concentrated and not diffuse. The papers date from 2013 onward and the underlying designs are older, so I do not see a timing problem. The citation is deliberately limited to the empirical analysis of adjustment. This leaves out the wider task-based theory literature, which has co-originators outside this ballot entry. The round-1 exchange did not change my view that, among the four leading candidates, B019 has the most directly tested central claims. It did make me more cautious about how much of the B019 case a citation can claim. I now treat this as a close call between B019, B001 and B020, not a clear lead.
statement.case_against: The magnitude and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, as are shift-share exposure designs. Several colleagues (Andersson, Hjalmarsson, Fredriksson) stress this, and I cannot dismiss it. Hjalmarsson and Fredriksson also point to the attribution risk from the task framework and the Acemoglu-Restrepo overlap, and to the Dorn-versus-Katz choice. The chair's observation that B019 has one explicit first-choice supporter, me, is a fair reminder that my weighting of design-based evidence is not shared widely. My own field gives me a bias toward transparent identification, and I may overweight it against framework breadth. B001 has the cleaner attribution and B020 the wider footprint in data and estimation. B019 has neither advantage. If the committee gives more weight to conceptual breadth or to attribution simplicity than I do, B019 should lose to one of them.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first and B019 second. She argues that mixed test results are the normal outcome for a testable framework, so they are not evidence that it failed. She also says B019 has a larger open attribution question, because of the Acemoglu-Restrepo overlap and the Katz-versus-Dorn choice.
responses.response: I accept the first point. A framework can earn recognition by making a question answerable even when estimates vary, and I have moved toward treating mixed empirical results as a weaker objection to B001 than I did in round 1. Where I still differ is weighting: when two candidates both have strong influence, I give extra weight to the one whose central claim has been tested directly and held. On attribution, I agree that B019 is messier overall. The mess comes mostly from the task-theory strand, though, and the citation I propose excludes that strand. For the China-shock evidence the core co-authorship is not in dispute. I therefore see the gap between B019 and B001 as narrower than my opening ranking suggested, and B001 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B016 first and B019 third, proposing only Autor and Hanson. He cites debate over exposure measures, shift-share identification and persistence. He also says the task framework has outside co-originators and that Katz overlaps with work already recognised.
responses.response: The chair asked whether Dorn belongs. My answer is yes, but only under a citation tied to the China-shock evidence on local labour markets. There the work is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson programme, and dropping Dorn would create the very attribution gap we are trying to avoid. If the committee insisted on a citation resting on the task framework, I would accept that Dorn's case is weaker and that a two-name Autor-Hanson version would be more coherent. I agree on the identification debate. My reading is that the shift-share literature has produced refinements and diagnostics, not a reversal, but that comes from my recollection and I have not verified it. I also agree that B016 is more bounded as a body of work. For me its weaker identification, which you concede, outweighs that advantage.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first. He argues that selection and reallocation mechanisms have been checked against firm-level data in many countries and are more empirically confirmed than protection for sale. He also flags the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum attribution gap.
responses.response: I find the empirical-confirmation argument for B020 the strongest challenge to my ordering, because it is the same criterion I use to rank B019 above B001. I therefore move B020 into my alternatives in place of B014, which received no real support in the exchange. I still keep it below B019. The credit boundary with the firm-level pioneers is unresolved and cannot be repaired within the credited list. B019's central credit is clearer. The chair asked whether I would accept either trade option. I could accept B020 and B001, and I would currently place B001 slightly ahead on attribution while B020 is ahead on empirical reach. I do not have a settled view between them.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B019 seventh and questions the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the split between the task and trade-shock work.
responses.response: I take both points. The debate over magnitude is real and it is why I describe the choice as close. I would still distinguish disagreement over size from doubt that the finding exists, and I do not think a prize citation needs to settle the long-run elasticity. A citation worded around adjustment and local labour markets claims the qualitative result and leaves the magnitudes to the literature. On the strands, I agree that the committee should not present trade and task as one achievement without saying so. That is why my citation names empirical analysis of adjustment to trade and technological change and not the task theory. If you think even that wording stitches two contributions together, that is a legitimate objection, and I cannot fully rebut it.

uncertainties: Whether the persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and the validity of shift-share designs, are settled enough for a prize citation. My belief that the qualitative result is robust rests on my recollection and the colleagues' openings, not on independent verification.

Whether a B019 citation about adjustment to trade and technological change describes one achievement or two, and whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. The answer depends on whether the citation rests on the China-shock papers or on the wider skill-demand and task work.
How the Acemoglu-Restrepo task literature, which lies outside the credited list, affects the technology half of the citation.
How to weigh design-based credibility against framework breadth and attribution simplicity. This is the main reason I rank B019 first while B001 and B020 are close behind.
Whether the committee would accept B001 or B020 as the trade option, and how Helpman's role in both should be framed. I do not have a firm view.
I have not independently verified citations, dates or priority claims. My assessments rest on my recollection of the literature and the written round-1 files.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship, institutional or editorial tie to any credited name on B019, B001 or B020 is apparent from my supplied profile. B014, my former second alternative, is no longer in my configuration. My research field values design-based, replicable evidence, which may bias me toward B019. I disclose this as a field preference, not a candidate tie, and discount it under the common criteria. My frequent co-authors, including Camerer, Johannesson, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber and Nosek, are not credited on any shortlisted ballot ID. I work with Abel Brodeur's Institute for Replication, which is not a candidate. Colleagues' files record collegial ties at SSE with committee members Andersson, Friberg and Strömberg. These are ties among committee members, not links to any candidate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
